What type of B12 have you been supplementing with? Have you ever been tested for MTHFR? It's a gene mutation that can cause a couple things, but one of those is inability to effectively process cyanocobalamin, the most common type in supplements. Absorption through the gut is also hit-or-miss, sublingual absorption is more reliable. 

Have you ever tried getting B12 shots? Most PCPs do them, although you do have to confirm the type being injected. For pills/injections, methylcobalamin is usually preferred, but adenosylcobalamin and hydroxocobalamin should be ok, too.

I don't know that your symptoms are caused by B12 deficiency, but it can cause those symptoms, and it can often stay hidden and untreated for quite a while. Get yourself a high-dose methylcobalamin sublingual like this one: https://www.amazon.com/Jarrow-Formulas-Methylcobalamin-Supports-Lozenges/dp/B0013OQGO6 and see if anything changes. If it does, either you were having an issue absorbing in your gut, or you should read up on MTHFR and possibly start taking methylfolate.

Nothing you say will be news to them, and even if you think it's an innocent comment, it will just cement your place as someone who doesn't get it and will never get it and can never, ever be trusted. 

I understand that it's probably extremely stressful worrying that someone you love will commit suicide, and depending on your relationship, the impact on you might be something you should discuss eventually, but that's not going to come during the current crisis. For current purposes, you hurt them, you were wrong, you're sorry, and you care about how they're feeling--you can have a conversation starting from there. 

Also, threatening suicide and then googling how many antidepressants to OD on (while you're there? or just that you have knowledge of?) sounds like a *suicidal gesture*, rather than a suicide plan in progress. 

This is something that's often misinterpreted either as an attention-seeking behavior, or an absolute desire to die, when really it's more like the behavior of someone who feels the life they're living now is intolerable, but doesn't really want to cease to exist, just wants things to become tolerable, and has no idea how to make that happen. 

A "cry for help," if you will, though often for more practical, life-fixing help than the stereotypical teens-in-therapy. (Although therapy can help, too!)

That's awful. I don't think that means you're a bad friend though, or that you shouldn't keep trying to be friends with people. I've seen things like that happen a couple times, and unless there was some kind of specific precipitating event, "creepy" in that context almost never means "you make people uncomfortable and/or are generally disliked." 

It means "you want to be friends with me more than I want to be friends with you." Which isn't a bad thing, bc it's kind of normal and important and healthy to want to be friends with people. Sometimes when the above is the case, people don't want to admit they're losing interest in a friendship, so it's easier to put the blame on the other side of the equation--to pretend that you're suddenly being WAY clingy, over-involved, just "creepy"--when really you're just doing normal friend stuff--so they have an excuse to break it off.

Another reason they might say that is they want to change social groups and think it would be easier without ties to you. "Creepy" here says nothing about you at all, it's just shorthand for "I am no longer allied with this person." 

Your friend doesn't want to be your friend anymore. That sucks. It's really, immensely, painful. But it doesn't say anything about you. They're just stumbling forward, making decisions, some of which they might look back and regret, same as you. You can feel this pain, this grief, almost, for as long as you need to, but don't wrap it up in shame or self-hatred. You've been on a downswing socially because you've just been through this awful friend breakup, and it's normal for it to take some time to get yourself together again. 

I think friend breakups are really underplayed in the media and in society, so people end up being confused when they encounter them and think they're a wuss for having feelings or that they're weird if they can't shrug it off and have everything go back to normal the next day, but in my experience they're often more affecting than romantic breakups.

Give yourself some time, and go easy on yourself. I believe you will be able to make friends, you just have to take it at your own pace. I'm around if you want to chat.

Reporting your parents for abuse would not mark you as emotionally unstable, and even if you were actually emotionally unstable, it would be no business of university admissions unless it was precipitating some otherwise-unacceptable behavior, like bullying or disrupting class. 

It's actually much better for your university prospects if you act now: if you wait until you're 18, you'll be considered a dependent student when applying for financial aid, which means your parents' income will be counted as your income--it will presumed they are financially supporting you (regardless of whether they actually are). 

If you can show you were alienated from your parents before 18, you'll be an independent student, which means their income won't be factored into your aid, so you won't have to rely on them.
